title: Middlebox inspection, TLS record bloat, and tail-latency impact
content:
Purpose and scope:

Quick notes + lab book for experiments exploring how middlebox/inspection behavior (NGFW/WAF/sidecar TLS-inspect) interacts with TLS record sizing and streaming protocols (gRPC/http2, http1.1 chunked) to amplify tail latency and CPU. Goal: find reproducible knobs we can surface as guidance or runtime defaults for hosted & dedicated deployments to avoid pathological amplification with small message workloads (typical LLM streaming: frequent small writes).

Why this matters:
- LLM inference streaming commonly emits many small token frames (10-200 bytes).
- Edge/proxy devices that perform TLS inspection (terminate+re-encrypt or deep packet inspection) often re-segment/re-record TLS, add extra buffering, or trigger syscall/coalescing behavior that changes the end-to-end timing semantics.
- Observed symptoms in prod-ish traces: 10–80ms sporadic spikes aligned with proxy hops; CPU jitter on proxy hosts; throughput cliffs under high concurrency.

High-level hypothesis:
- Certain TLS record sizes + middlebox inspection modes produce extra copies and syscall boundaries that turn many small writes into fewer larger TLS records or interleaved re-encrypts, causing queueing and head-of-line delays for other concurrent streams on the same connection.
- HTTP/2 SETTINGS, frame packing, and gRPC keepalives interact with this, making gRPC (multiplexed) more or less sensitive depending on implementation details of the middlebox.

Testbed (simple, reproducible):
- Client pod (streambench v0.8): opens N concurrent streams to server via proxy. Client emits token-sized writes on a 15–30ms cadence to emulate generation.
- Proxy: Envoy (v1.25) configured in two modes: TLS passthrough, TLS terminate+re-encrypt (INSPECT), and with an inline Lua filter to simulate per-record inspection CPU.
- Middlebox variant: a simulated NGFW (userland process) that reads records, optionally delays 0–5ms per record, and re-writes with different record size semantics.
- Server: model endpoint (dummy echo) accepting http2/gRPC and returning stream ack.
- Network: tc/netem to model 5ms baseline RTT, 0.5ms jitter; separate runs with 20ms RTT to amplify head-of-line effects.

Key knobs we swept:
- TLS record maximum payloads: 256B, 512B, 1KB, 2KB, 16KB (i.e., typical openssl max)
- Client write sizes: 64B (small token), 256B, 1KB
- Concurrency: 1, 8, 32 streams per connection
- Protocol: http1.1-chunked vs http2 (grpc native + grpc-web over http2)
- Proxy mode: passthrough vs terminate+inspect vs terminate+re-encrypt with random per-record re-segmentation
- Middlebox per-record delay: 0ms, 0.5ms, 2ms

Microbenchmark harness notes (commands we used):
- streambench invocation (custom harness):
  ./streambench --target https://proxy:8443/echo --streams 8 --write-size 64 --cadence 20ms --duration 300s --protocol http2 --tls-record-max 512
- Envoy bootstrap snippets: included below in repo PR. Key change: tls_context->max_fragment_length simulated via BoringSSL shim in env test image (see PR).
- netem: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 5ms 0.5ms distribution normal

Representative results (median of 5 runs, 300s each; percentiles reported):
- Baseline: passthrough, tls-record-max=16KB, client write=64B, streams=8, protocol=http2
  - p50 latency (first token): 6.8ms; p95: 9.5ms; p99: 18.2ms
- Terminate+inspect, middlebox-delay=0ms, tls-record-max=16KB
  - p50: 8.1ms; p95: 16.7ms; p99: 45.3ms (tail amplification present)
- Terminate+inspect, tls-record-max=512B, client write=64B, streams=8
  - p50: 9.8ms; p95: 32.1ms; p99: 210.4ms (severe pathology)
- Passthrough but proxy does re-encrypt with forced 256B records (simulate re-segmentation)
  - p50: 8.9ms; p95: 28.9ms; p99: 180.0ms
- HTTP/1.1 chunked, same settings as above, streams=8
  - p50: 10.2ms; p95: 35.7ms; p99: 230ms (HTTP/1.1 slightly worse due to per-chunk flush semantics and proxy buffering)

CPU observations:
- Proxy CPU per-request increases with record-count (many small records => more crypto ops and user-space copies). On c5.large-equivalent test VMs, the proxy CPU consumption doubled when moving from 16KB records to 512B records at 32 streams.
- When the inspection filter adds 0.5–2ms delay per record (simulate regex/deep-inspect), the additional latency compounds non-linearly because multiplexed streams share the same TLS connection and block on write serialization in the re-encrypt code path.

Trace decomposition (devtools / pcap / tcpdump summary):
- Symptom: client writes small frames rapidly, proxy coalesces into larger TLS records only after a re-encrypt buffer threshold or on flush heartbeat. That coalescing sometimes waits for N frames or a timeout (e.g., 10ms), adding jitter.
- For gRPC/http2 multiplexed scenario: one stream getting a large re-encrypt-induced delay causes other streams to see increased latency due to the single-threaded re-encrypt serialization in our Envoy test shim.

Hypothesis validation experiments (what we ran to confirm):
- Force proxy to preserve client record boundaries (no re-segmentation): tail improved ~3x in the 512B case.
- Turn off TLS inspection (passthrough): tail improved but client-side saw more TCP-level retransmits when we raised concurrent connections due to lack of Nagle suppression in the client harness; so passthrough is not a silver bullet in all network setups.
- Increase client-side write coalescing (emit larger writes on client): tail collapses to baseline; suggests fixing at client SDK level (pack tokens into 512B writes) reduces pathologies dramatically.

Practical recommendations for Redwood runtime and SDKs (short-term):
1) SDK-level batching: default token wire framing to prefer 256–512B writes when safe; add a batching config exposed on the API (e.g., streaming_coalesce_target_bytes = 512).
2) Server and edge: detect middlebox re-encrypt (tls reneg/changing record sizes) via telemetry; if detected, prefer shorter-lived connections or different keepalive pacing to avoid head-of-line amplification across streams.
3) Envoy/sidecar guidance: add option to preserve client record boundaries when acting as TLS passthrough or re-encrypt (config flag: preserve_client_record_boundaries=true). Document tradeoffs: less CPU for re-encrypt, possible higher number of small TLS records on the tunnel side.
4) Instrumentation: add per-token latency histogram in trace where we correlate token emission -> TLS record transmit timestamp -> TLS record receive timestamp at server to identify re-segmentation.

Longer-term:
- Consider offloading re-encrypt/inspection to separate worker pool to avoid per-connection serialization of crypto operations; parallelize re-encrypt per-record without blocking other streams.
- Evaluate adaptive client pacing: detect pathological middlebox (based on p99 delta) and automatically increase coalescing target.
- Discuss with infra partners a best-practice for dedicated deployments: avoid inline TLS inspection on inference paths where token-level streaming latency matters.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How common are the commercial NGFW behaviors that re-segment records in our customer fleet? Need telemetry sweep across obsv logs to classify (JIRA INF-912).
- Are there regulatory/security requirements that force inspection in certain regions/customers, making SDK changes the only viable mitigation?
- How does QUIC (TLS 1.3 over UDP) change the failure modes? Hypothesis: QUIC's packetization and connection-level multiplexing may reduce some re-encrypt head-of-line behavior but could expose other amplification patterns (we should test with quic-go or msquic).

Raw data pointers and artifacts:
- streambench run artifacts: s3://ci-artifacts/streambench/middlebox-inspect/oct-2025/ (raw pcap, traces, scripts)
- plot scripts: github.com/redwood-inference/streambench/tree/main/plots/middlebox_inspect
- envoy-test-config and dumb-inspector: PR #42 in streambench repo (linked above)

Next immediate steps (this week):
- Add SDK coalescing flag + telemetry toggle to streambench; run against 5 customer-config proxies (Noah to coordinate).
- Collect fleet telemetry of TLS record size distributions at ingress (Evelyn to draft query).
- Prototype per-connection re-encrypt worker queue (Diego to spike) and measure p99 impact under 32-stream workloads.

Notes to self (lower friction / messy):
- Observed an outlier run where p99 hit >800ms: that correlated with a mid-run Envoy reload (config update) and re-keying; shows coupling between management plane operations and tail latency.
- Keep in mind: not every proxy or NGFW behaves the same; some preserve client records, others will always re-segment to their internal MTU or policy. Hard to generalize but we can provide clear mitigations.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing locally
- Build streambench: go build ./cmd/streambench
- Start envoy test image: docker run -p 8443:8443 redwood/envoy-test:tls-reseg-shim
- Start dumb-inspector: ./dumb-inspector --listen 8444 --reseg-size 256 --delay 1ms
- Run: ./streambench --target https://localhost:8443/echo --streams 8 --write-size 64 --cadence 20ms --duration 120s --protocol http2 --tls-record-max 512

If you want I can split this into a formal runbook and a one-pager for infra + SDK teams. For now leaving this as a lab book + action list.

-- Priya
